units.translation: Thus Bamberger corrected what is in M: καὶ τὰ χρέα ἔπη [and the useful words], changed by Turnebus to τὰ χρεῖ᾽ ἔπη [the useful words]. In a different sense Theocr. 25, 6 said ὁδοῦ ζαχρεῖον ὁδίτην [a traveler in need of the road]: which is the usual meaning of the adjective χρεῖος [needy], as Aeschylus himself a little later at v. 202 said χρεῖος εἶ ξένη φυγάς [you are a needy stranger, an exile]. Different is the Homeric ζαχρηής [very useful], written ζαχρειής [very useful] by some and explained differently by others, on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 10.
Answer the strangers with words of reverence, lamentation, and great need.

to live
Aeschylus used only a few forms of this verb. Present ζῶ ζῇς ζῶμεν ζῶσι, infinitive ζῆν, participle ζῶν ζῶσα, imperfect ἔζων third person ἔζη. I live.
καὶ ζῶντα καὶ βλέποντα [both living and seeing], where now χλωρόν τε καὶ β [pale and seeing] from the gloss of Hesychius, about which see under χλωρός [pale].
θυηλαὶ [sacrificial offerings] Herm., i.e. they flourish.

Thus M, not ζεύγλησι [the yoke-straps], which is in some copies, where Hermann says: "ζεύγλην [the yoke-strap] some say is the curvature of the yoke, others the part into which the neck of the animal is inserted, or, what is the same, the straps, which are called subiugia by the Latins. In this sense Aeschylus used it here, and before him Homer Il. 19, 405 πᾶσα δὲ χαίτη ζεύγλης ἐξεριποῦσα παρὰ ζυγὸν | οὐδας ἵκανεν [all the mane, slipping from the yoke-strap, reached the ground]. See the Homeric scholiasts and Scheffer on vehicles p. 116 ff."
